caseStudy.label: Case study
caseStudy.title: Property-document checker
caseStudy.summary: A legal workspace that helps surface issues in land documents before they become expensive problems.

sections.title: Context
sections.body: An early-stage legal-tech startup was building an AI workspace for lawyers. I was the designer on the project, working directly with the founders.

sections.title: User and problem
sections.body: Checking land documents for issues can take lawyers weeks. The idea was a checker that flags problems early, so a lawyer’s time goes to judgment instead of searching.

sections.title: Options
sections.body: We looked at three directions: a general chat interface, a checklist-style review, and a document view with issues flagged in place.

sections.title: What I cut
sections.body: The founders’ feature list was long. I questioned each item against one question: does this help a lawyer decide faster? Most did not.
sections.note: Why: a smaller first version was easier to test and easier to trust.

sections.title: Tradeoffs
sections.body: Fewer features at launch meant some requests had to wait. The check also had to be clear about what it was unsure of, because a wrong ‘all clear’ costs more than a missed flag.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.body: I don’t have usage metrics for this feature. If I were measuring it, I would look at time to first review and how often flagged issues were accepted.

sections.title: What I’d change
sections.body: I’d put real documents in front of lawyers earlier, before settling the flow.

howIWork.label: How I work
howIWork.body: I start with the problem and the person who has it. I question long feature lists, because most of them are guesses. I like to see how a decision moves through a whole system, not just one screen, and I want to know afterwards whether it worked.
